# RiboPilot <a href="https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/"><img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="138" /></a>

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

RiboPilot recovers the **nuclear ribosomal repeat (nrDNA)** from genome skimming data, then helps you check and clean up the result and package it for submission to GenBank. It is a companion to [MitoPilot](https://github.com/Smithsonian/MitoPilot), which does the same thing for the mitochondrial genome. You can run both on the same samples and get both marker sets from one sequencing run.

You do not need to be a programmer to use RiboPilot. Most of your work happens in a **point-and-click app** that runs in your web browser. The step-by-step [Get started guide](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/RiboPilot.html) walks through a complete project from start to finish.

# What RiboPilot recovers

Every cell carries the ribosomal RNA genes in a repeated unit that is copied hundreds to thousands of times in a row. Because there are so many copies, even a shallow, inexpensive "genome skim" sequences this region very deeply, essentially for free. RiboPilot reconstructs that repeat:

```
  ETS       18S      ITS1   5.8S   ITS2         28S         IGS
~~~~~~|============|~~~~~~|======|~~~~~~|================|~~~~~~
          (SSU)                               (LSU)
```

This is one copy of the repeat; copies follow one another head to tail, hundreds of times. SSU and LSU are the small and large subunit genes (18S and 28S). ITS is ITS1, 5.8S, and ITS2 together. ETS and IGS are spacers outside the genes; the IGS of one copy runs into the ETS of the next.

From it you get the most widely used nuclear markers for phylogenetics and DNA barcoding: **18S**, **28S**, **ITS1**, **ITS2**, and the full **ITS** region.

The three ribosomal genes (18S, 5.8S, 28S) are highly conserved and act as anchors. The two spacers (ITS1, ITS2) sit between them, evolve quickly, and are the regions that distinguish closely related species.

# What RiboPilot does for you

The app walks each project through five steps, in order:

1. **Taxonomy.** RiboPilot matches the `Taxon` you give each sample to the NCBI taxonomy, using a local copy, and you check and lock each match. Samples must be reviewed and locked here before they move on to assembly, so the taxonomy that guides scoring and curation is one you have signed off on. The first time, RiboPilot downloads about 80 MB and builds an index of about 0.5 GB in the project, which takes a few minutes.
2. **Reference.** RiboPilot groups related samples and builds a reference database of known rDNA sequences for each group, from GenBank.
3. **Assemble.** One run cleans the reads, assembles the ribosomal repeat for each sample, picks the best assembly path, finds the five features (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S), and checks each result for problems such as a missing gene, an unusual length, a possible contaminant, or a chimera. You keep or drop contigs and lock the samples you are happy with.
4. **Annotation Review.** You check the features and quality flags of each kept contig, adjust boundaries if needed, and lock it.
5. **Export.** RiboPilot writes a tidy, GenBank-ready submission package, and asks about any flagged record first.

Behind the scenes RiboPilot uses established bioinformatics tools ([fastp](https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp), [GetOrganelle](https://github.com/Kinggerm/GetOrganelle), [barrnap](https://github.com/tseemann/barrnap) / [pybarrnap](https://github.com/moshi4/pybarrnap), [ITSx](https://microbiology.se/software/itsx/), [BLAST](https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi), and others) and stitches them together for you. You do not need to learn or run any of them yourself.

# Taxonomic Scope

Each group of samples, fishes included, needs a reference database of known rDNA sequences. You build it once per group in the app, from GenBank; see the [reference database guide](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/Reference-Databases.html).

It also runs automatic quality checks tuned for a taxonomic group. Five settings ship, picked from each sample's lineage: a generic animal setting, and settings for ray-finned fishes, sea stars, true jellyfish, and octocorals; see the [curation guide](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/Curation-Flags.html).

# Installation

RiboPilot needs Docker (or Singularity on a cluster), Java, Nextflow, and R. The [Installation guide](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/Installation.html) lists versions and checks. Then, in R:

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("dmacguigan/RiboPilot")
```

# Getting started

The best way to learn RiboPilot is to run the built-in test project. The first command downloads the test samples and sets everything up; the second opens the app:

```r
RiboPilot::new_test_project(path = "~/ribopilot_test")
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("~/ribopilot_test")
```

By default this fetches small rDNA-filtered read subsets published with the RiboPilot releases, so setup takes under a minute. Pass `full_size = TRUE` to download the complete read sets from ENA/SRA instead (several GB). The first run also downloads the container image once (about 2.6 GB).

From there, the [Get started guide](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/RiboPilot.html) walks you through the five steps in the app.

# Citing RiboPilot

Run `citation("RiboPilot")` in R. The [Citing RiboPilot](https://dmacguigan.github.io/RiboPilot/articles/Citing.html) page lists the tools RiboPilot runs, with their versions and references, for your methods section.
